I. INTRODUCTION
The advent of neural network (NN) has greatly enhanced and revolutionized the Artificial Intelligence. Even though the
research of neural network can be traced back to early 1980 by Hinton et al., its power began to appear only in recent decades.
NN model has been immersed in many area of AI including cv, nlp, speech and reinforcement learning etc. and has witnessed
thrill and many recent breakthroughs in AI development. Although realistic NN works very well, unfortunately, it still defies
rigorous mathematical understanding.
Recently there are a surge of research on theoretic foundation of NN. One of them is regarding the training dynamics in
neural network especially for stochastic gradient descent algorithm. For example, [Jin et al., 2017] shows that noise SGD can
escape from saddle points. [Fang et al., 2019] explains that SGD can also escape from saddle points in a large probability. Many
works [Arora et al., 2019, Bao et al., 2023, Du et al., 2019, 2018, Mertikopoulos et al., 2020, Rotskoff and Vanden-Eijnden,
2022, Zhou et al., 2019] show that SGD can converge to global minimal points under certain conditions.
To tackle this problem one way is to consider its continuous version, that is, to come up with an appropriate definition of
continuous limitation when the width or depth approach to infinity, and study the training dynamics of SGD in such limitation.

differential equation problem that forms a beautiful mathematical framework and so can leverage strong mathematical tools to
solve them. The original discrete version can be recovered and derived lastly by sampling from some probability distributions
or discretization of the continuous or differentiable equations.

a trained neural network. This can be either under the assumption that the network is trained by some specific optimization

generalization property of a general two-layer ReLU neural work. It doesn’t require specific network structure constraints
assumed in other works and derives a nonasymptotic near optimal generalization error bound. A closely related work to theirs’
is [Neyshabur et al.].
However, as far as we know, the rigorous study (rather than empirical or heuristic study) of generalization property for
multilayer neural networks is few, albeit there are many work providing generalization error bound in various way and it
indeed looks like a puzzle for readers to understand their complex relations. One shallow reason is that the two-layer ReLU
neural network is quite close to a linear function that makes it easier to be transferred to traditional and well studied statistical
problems, whereas multilayer neural network is highly nonlinear and nonconvex.

we propose what we think a satisfactory generalization theory for multilayer neual networks should be, described in the
next section. This paper tries to fill the gap between theory and practice by giving a quite general rigorous characterization
of the generalization property of a general multilayer neural network for quite general problems including regressions and
classifications, with almost trivial assumptions. If the activation is ReLU, our bound is near optimal up to a logarithm factor.

endeavor, we have found a byproduct to overcome the difficulties in establishing the so called path enhanced ridge-lasso duality

bound the empirical errors. When applying this method to two-layer neural networks we get a greatly simplified proof. This
strategy requires neither dividing the weights into groups nor exploration of symmetry property between optimal weights in
the same groups, as in [Wang and Lin, 2023]. Another work that is mostly related to our work is perhaps [Parhi and Nowak,
2022]. They set up a correct space of functions of second-order bounded variation in the Radon domain, which turns out to
be the same as the variation space [Siegel and Xu, 2023] studied before, for associating shallow ReLU neural networks and
same form of learning problem, and finally establish the similar conclusion with us in this space. One novel difference is that

proof of L2 generalization error is metric entropy argument corresponding to methods in underparametrization regime of ours,
however, to us it will not be optimal as aforementioned reason: overparametrization and underparametrization are different.
The main contribution of this work can be summarized as follows.
1) We give a first near complete non-asymptotic generalization error for multilayer neural networks, with no any constraint
on network structure (e.g. intrinsic sparsity or boundeness of certain norms), no constraint on any particular activation
function, no constraint on any particular optimization algorithm used, and no boundness assumption on the loss. And we
explicitly model the target function space and take the approximation error into account. The latter point is notable as it is
almost ignored in previous works.
2) We explicitly distinguish between overparametrised regime and underparametrised regime, and estimate the generalization
error separately, obtaining a result that is as better as possible. Previous works either give a single bound thus is not
optimal at all or focus on overparametrization only.
3) When the activation function is ReLU and loss is MSE, we show that our generalization bound is near-optimal, i.e. up to
a logarithmic factor, by establishing an information theoretic lower bound.
4) We establish an approximation bound for multilayer neural networks with Lipschitz activation in a suitable continuous
function space called generalized Barron space, greatly strengthen previous known result. To our best knowledge, this
result is new.
5) We show that the generalization upper bound can predict the double descent phenomenon. We don’t realize any other
non-asymptotic bounds having such implication.
The organization of this paper is as follows: In section 2 we discuss some relevant works. Section 3 is the notation statement.
In section 4 we set up a reasonable function space we work on in this paper. We define the appropriate normed function space
to set a framework to study general problem modelled by multilayer neural network; In section 5 we setup the learning problem
under consideration and the optimization objects; Section 6 studies the approximation properties of this function space; Section 7,
8, 9 and 10 study the empirical and generalization error bound in overparametrised and underparametrised regimes, respectively,
and discuss its implication of double descent phenomenon. Section 11 generalize our theory to Lipschitz loss functions with
some very mild conditions. We compare our result with other existing results in section 12 and show our superiority. Finally in
section 13 we conclude our paper. All technique details including all proofs are presented in supplementary information. We
additionally show the collinearity of weights of the optimal solution for multilayer ReLU network in there, which is also new.

We review relevant work to study generalization properties of two-layer and multilayer neural networks, and discuss the
relations and differences with our work. We strongly suggest the readers to consult [Wang and Lin, 2023] and references therein

first for thorough discussions of the background and motivation of this problem and several relations with other related theories,
e.g. high dimensional statistics and recent understanding of bias-variance tradeoff [Derumigny and Schmidt-Hieber, 2023].
Neural Tangent Kernel [Chizat et al., 2019, Jacot et al., 2018] is a method to understand the training dynamics of NN by
formulating it as kernel gradient descent with neural tangent kernel. When the number of neurons approaching infinity, this
kernel is constant during training, thus favoring the easy analysis. This method requires the parameters staying in a small
neiborhood of initial values, which doesn’t align with realistic NN. The generalization analysis is therefore not useful.
Mean field theory [Rotskoff and Vanden-Eijnden, 2022, Sirignano and Spiliopoulos, 2020] aims to formulate the training
dynamics of NN as a stochastic partial differential equation in continuous limit. The generalization property analysis via SPDE
poses difficulties that doesn’t seem to be easy to solve.
There are a number of literature making the analysis of generalization properties of two-layer neural network. Most of them
leaverage large number law or central limit theorem to represent training dynamics of SGD as a stochastic partial differential
equation in continuous limit. [Mei et al., 2018] proposes a mean field analysis of training dynamics of two-layer NN via SGD
by recasting it as a SPDE in continuous limit. However, it is not clear how this method can be generalized to multilayer NN,
the analysis of the resulting SPDE is by far an easy task unless under specific cases, the generalization property analysis is
therefore also tough.
Since the discovery of double descent phenomenon [Belkin et al., 2019], there were many works trying to theoretically
understand this under various assumptions. [Belkin et al., 2020, Hastie et al., 2022, Muthukumar et al., 2020] started detailed
analysis for classical linear models or other simple models,e.g. random feature model which is equivalent to two layer neural
network with the first layer parameters fixed. Another line of attacking this problem is to do asymptotic analysis for these
models [Deng et al., 2022, Liang and Sur, 2022, Mei and Montanari, 2022, Yang et al., 2020],i.e., letting the depth, width,
dimension and number of training data approaching infinity separately or jointly. Random matrix theory is largely leveraged by
these works. By this theory, they can find the explicit generalization error expressions in the asymptotic regime and showed its
curve with respect to the structural parameter demonstrates the ”double descent” shape. In this line a lower generalization
error bound for two layer neural network is also developed in [Seroussi and Zeitouni, 2022]. Notably, a “multiple descent”
phenomenon in infinite-dimensional linear regression and kernel ridgeless regression is proposed in [Li and Meng, 2021, Liang
et al., 2020]. Despite these advances, it is still unclear how these simple models can be helpful or insightful for multilayer NN
model. The gap between them is potentially large in our opinion. The reader can also check a very recent thorough discussions
of double descent [Schaeffer et al., 2023].
Several works derived the generalization property for two-layer neural networks in certain variation spaces [Bach, 2017, Parhi
and Nowak, 2021, 2022]. Most of the existing work focuses on variational formulations of the empirical risk minimization
problem. However, the network width of the solution is required to be smaller than the sample size, which doesn’t fall in our
regime of overparametrised NN. Another attempt [E et al., 2019] allows the network width grows to infinity, however, the l1
path norm regularization induces potentially sparsity in parameters, which seems doesn’t have implications for intrinsically
overparametrised NN.
For deep neural network, there are some empirical analysis towards the phenomenon aspects of generalization ability. One
of the most surprising feature that any deep neural network with the number of parameters greater than the number of data
points has perfect finite sample expressivity renders rethinking what generalization means [Zhang et al., 2021]. [Nagarajan and
Kolter, 2019] empirically found that the generalization crucially depends on a notion of model capacity that is restricted through
implicit regularization of l2 distance from the initialization. [Neyshabur et al., 2017a] discussed different candidate complexity
measures that might explain generalization in neural networks. It also outlines a concrete methodology for investigating such
measures, and report on experiments studying how well the measures explain different phenomena. [Schiff et al., 2021, Zhao
and Zhang, 2021] propose some new measures e.g. spasity, Gi-score and Pal-score, that can explicitly calculate and compare
generalization ability. A deep insight was analyzed in [Neyshabur et al., 2017a] where they show quantitative evidence, based
on representational geometry, of when and where memorization occurs, and link double descent to increasing object manifold
dimensionality.
To the knowledge of the authors, an incomplete list for rigorous generalization theory for multilayer neural network
is [Allen-Zhu et al., 2019, Bartlett et al., 2017, 2019, Gu et al., 2023, Jakubovitz et al., 2019, Neyshabur et al., 2017b, 2018,
Tirumala, Wang and Ma, 2022]. Early classical work [Bartlett et al., 2017, 2019, Neyshabur et al., 2017b, Tirumala] bounds the
generalization error by using some complexity measures like VC dimension, Rademacher complexity and Bayesian PCA, etc. It
is well known that these methods often require the loss function being bounded, which is not practical. As classical theory
focuses on bounding the generalization error by empirical erros and other complexity quantity related to neural networks, it
doesn’t pay attention to the estimations of empirical error, meaning that it doesn’t offer complete picture on the generalization
error. These bounds are also not optimal as they don’t distinguish between overparametrization and underparametrization.

The main reason why our work is different from others is that we don't require any constraints on the loss function, which
makes our bound applicable to a broader range of loss functions, including non-Lipschitz and even non-continuous ones. Moreover,
we explicitly model the target function space and take the approximation error into account. The latter point is critical as it is
almost ignored in previous works.

the Lipschitz constant, i.e., the smallest L such that ||f(x)−f(y)|| ≤ L||x−y|| for all x, y. For any function f, we denote

For any function f, we denote the minimal L2 norm of the approximating function as ||f||_L2. We also denote the minimal
Lipschitz constant of the function as ||f||_Lip.

For any x ∈ R^d, we denote ||x|| as its Euclidean norm. For any matrix X, we denote ||X|| as its spectral norm and

IV. SET UP OF FUNCTION SPACE
In this section, we define the function space F, which is the set of functions f: R^d → R that can be expressed as f(x) = σ(Wx + b),
where σ is the activation function, and W and b are the parameters. We assume that the activation function σ is Lipschitz continuous
with constant Lσ, and that ReLU is a special case.

V. SET UP OF LEARNING PROBLEM
We consider the problem of learning a function f: R^d → R from a set of m training samples (xi, yi), i = 1, ..., m. The goal is
to find a function f that minimizes the empirical risk, defined as 1/m sum_{i=1}^m L(f(xi), yi), where L is the loss function.

The optimization object is the function f that minimizes the empirical risk over a set of parameters. We denote the optimal function as
f*, which may be the true target function or an approximation to it.

models [Deng et al., 2022, Liang and Sur, 2022, Mei and Montanari, 2022, Yang et al., 2020],i.e., letting the depth, width,
dimension and number of training data approaching infinity separately or jointly. Random matrix theory is largely leveraged by
these works. By this theory, they can find the explicit generalization error expressions in the asymptotic regime and showed its
curve with respect to the structural parameter demonstrates the ”double descent” shape. In this line a lower generalization
error bound for two layer neural network is also developed in [Seroussi and Zeitouni, 2022]. Notably, a “multiple descent”
phenomenon in infinite-dimensional linear regression and kernel ridgeless regression is proposed in [Li and Meng, 2021, Liang
et al., 2020]. Despite these advances, it is still unclear how these simple models can be helpful or insightful for multilayer NN
model. The gap between them is potentially large in our opinion. The reader can also check a very recent thorough discussions
of double descent [Schaeffer et al., 2023].
Several works derived the generalization property for two-layer neural networks in certain variation spaces [Bach, 2017, Parhi
and Nowak, 2021, 2022]. Most of the existing work focuses on variational formulations of the empirical risk minimization
problem. However, the network width of the solution is required to be smaller than the sample size, which doesn’t fall in our
regime of overparametrised NN. Another attempt [E et al., 2019] allows the network width grows to infinity, however, the l1
path norm regularization induces potentially sparsity in parameters, which seems doesn’t have implications for intrinsically
overparametrised NN.
For deep neural network, there are some empirical analysis towards the phenomenon aspects of generalization ability. One
of the most surprising feature that any deep neural network with the number of parameters greater than the number of data
points has perfect finite sample expressivity renders rethinking what generalization means [Zhang et al., 2021]. [Nagarajan and
Kolter, 2019] empirically found that the generalization crucially depends on a notion of model capacity that is restricted through
implicit regularization of l2 distance from the initialization. [Neyshabur et al., 2017a] discussed different candidate complexity
measures that might explain generalization in neural networks. It also outlines a concrete methodology for investigating such
measures, and report on experiments studying how well the measures explain different phenomena. [Schiff et al., 2021, Zhao
and Zhang, 2021] propose some new measures e.g. spasity, Gi-score and Pal-score, that can explicitly calculate and compare
generalization ability. A deep insight was analyzed in [Neyshabur et al., 2017a] where they show quantitative evidence, based
on representational geometry, of when and where memorization occurs, and link double descent to increasing object manifold
dimensionality.
To the knowledge of the authors, an incomplete list for rigorous generalization theory for multilayer neural network
is [Allen-Zhu et al., 2019, Bartlett et al., 2017, 2019, Gu et al., 2023, Jakubovitz et al., 2019, Neyshabur et al., 2017b, 2018,
Tirumala, Wang and Ma, 2022]. Early classical work [Bartlett et al., 2017, 2019, Neyshabur et al., 2017b, Tirumala] bounds the
generalization error by using some complexity measures like VC dimension, Rademacher complexity and Bayesian PCA, etc. It
is well known that these methods often require the loss function being bounded, which is not practical. As classical theory
focuses on bounding the generalization error by empirical erros and other complexity quantity related to neural networks, it
doesn’t pay attention to the estimations of empirical error, meaning that it doesn’t offer complete picture on the generalization
error. These bounds are also not optimal as they don’t distinguish between overparametrization and underparametrization
regimes that should have fundamental differences as the salient double descent phenomenon indicates, and so the upper bound
will never predict double descent phenomenon. [Tirumala] doesn’t rely on aforementioned complexity norm but use direct
analytic analysis to establish concentration inequality that is, in spirit, similar to our methods, but it still requires the boundness
of loss function and not optimal due to the same reason. For recent work, a kind of generalization error bound analysis appears
in [Gu et al., 2023], but it is for two and three layer neural networks only and studies how generalization error converges under

4
gradient descent algorithm. [Wang and Ma, 2022] provides a generalization error bound for multilayer neural networks under
stochastic gradient descent algorithm. Again, it is focused on a specific optimization algorithm. Furthermore, these two works
don’t consider the target function space, which means they don’t take into account the approximation errors, and don’t estimate
the empirical errors. The second work also puts boundness constraint of certain norm of multilayer neural networks. Our work
differs from theirs’ in that we don’t require knowing the optimization algorithm beforehand, don’t put any structural constraint
on the multilayer neural networks and integrate the target function space and thus approximation error into our generalization
bound expression.
After reviewing the aforementioned work, we find that the generalization theories they find either deal with two-layer neural
networks, consider only asymptotic regime, put structure constraints on neural networks, depend on particular optimization
algorithms, require boundness of loss function or are not aware of potential differences between underparametrization and
overparametrization so are not predicative of double descent phenomenon, and don’t consider approximation error aprior. If we
just consider how our estimator performs on test set, then it is fine to only estimate the difference between generalization and
empirical errors for such estimator, as standard Rademacher based bounds do. However, if we want to see how difference our
estimator compared with true model, in which case, in our opinion, it is a more accurate metric and ultimate goal of machine
learning, we have to consider the true model into place and the corresponding empirical error, then, is not exactly computable
from running experiments only. Through inspecting people’s experience in deep learning in recent decades, we propose here
what we think a satisfactory generalization theory there should be. We call a set of generalization error expressions or bounds
for multilayer neural networks complete if
1) it measures the difference between the estimated model and the true model in a nonasymptotic fashion;
2) all terms in the expressions or bounds are computable without running the experiments first, meaning that it has to do
with estimation of empirical error;
3) it applies to all realistic neural networks without essential constraints on their structures, e.g. sparsity, boundess of some
norms or asymptotic regime;
4) it sheds light to the observed double descent phenomenon in practice (otherwise it is not aligned with the reality and not
optimal);
5) it applies to most of common activation functions in practice;
6) it applies to most of common loss functions in practive, in particular, it doesn’t require the boundness of loss functions, as
most of common losses are not bounded;
7) it applies to most of common optimization algorithms in practice.
Regarding to point 7, it is certainly valuable having results for a particular optimization algorithm, however, it is not the point
of this paper. Although the aforementioned empirical findings and partial results are necessary steps toward better understanding
of generalization property of NN, no established even near complete theory has been public to community for the simplest
deep NN: multilayer ReLU NN.
